name: Lunda
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 3 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Kashoki, Mubanga E. & Michael Mann. 1978. A general sketch of the Bantu languages of Zambia. In Sirarpi Ohannessian & Mubanga E. Kashoki (eds.), Language in Zambia, 47-100. London: International African Institute (for the Survey of Language Use and Language Teaching in Eastern Africa). Open: UNZA DSpace item 123456789/939. Recording-locality paragraph (p. 107) from the same volume, ch. 3: Lehmann, D. A. 1978. Languages of the Kafue Basin: introductory notes. In Language in Zambia, 101ff.
catalog_locator: Sec. 3.4 'Tone and Stress', pp. 70-71: the stress paragraph and the statement that every syllable carries tone are on p. 70, the two-tone sentence runs across the p. 70/71 break (the tone-pair table there is elided), and the Lunda tone example 'bark of a tree' is on p. 71. Scope sentence ('patterns common among all Zambian languages as illustrated by the languages which we studied'): sec. 3.0 'Sound Systems of Zambian Languages', p. 62 (the section opens on p. 61). Penultimate-lengthening rule: sec. 3.1, pp. 63-64. Lunda (Ndembu) and Lunda (Ishindi) among the 25 varieties studied: Table 2:1, p. 54 (the chapter runs pp. 47-100). Recording locality ('The recordings were made in Solwezi'): not in the Kashoki & Mann chapter but in ch. 3, D. A. Lehmann, 'Languages of the Kafue Basin: introductory notes' (pp. 101ff.), sec. 4.5 'Lunda', p. 107.
catalog_quote: In Zambian languages, in contrast, syllables are more or less evenly stressed, i.e. they are pronounced with almost the same degree of prominence or force. In some languages, however, (e.g. Cewa) the penultimate syllable seems to be pronounced with slightly greater force than the rest of the syllables in the same word. However, it must be remembered that that is also the syllable, according to the rule mentioned earlier, which is lengthened, so that the stress may be the effect of the lengthening of the vowel. In any case, independent of the lengthening of vowels, stress in Zambian languages does not distinguish words from each other in meaning. A characteristic feature of all Zambian languages is that each of their syllables carries tone. ... There are only two contrastive tones in Zambian languages, high and low, which serve to distinguish ... between words which are otherwise identical in all other respects. ... The significance of tone in Zambian languages may be seen from the following examples: ... "bark of a tree" (Lunda)
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: The quotation was checked again. Opened and the full UNZA scanned bundle (22,098 lines). Sec. 3.4 'Tone and Stress' begins at the scanned text; the quoted passage runs lines 3185-3196, under the page header '70 LANGUAGES OF ZAMBIA' and before 'SKETCH OF THE BANTU LANGUAGES 71' (line 3203), so the locator pp. 70-71 is right. The quote is present word for word; the only differences are scanned artefacts that the report silently normalised: 'vv'->'w' (declared), plus 'syilable'->'syllable' (twice) and 'hovvever'->'however' (not declared). No words added, dropped or reordered. The Lunda tone example '"barkofatree"(Lunda)' is at line 3212 (p. 71), as stated. READING. The section says: Zambian la…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No word-stress rule: Lunda, like the other Zambian Bantu languages the survey studied, has syllables of roughly equal prominence; any extra force on the penult is attributed to (non-contrastive) penultimate vowel lengthening, which the same chapter (pp. 63-64) says is a standard rule in the Eastern-Province languages and 'several languages of the Northwestern Province' (Lunda's province, not named). Stress is never lexically distinctive; the language is tonal (H vs L on every syllable; Lunda tone example on p. 71; Kawasha 2008: 42 confirms grammatical H tone marks Lunda subject relatives).
new_statements.exceptions: Penultimate prominence 'in some languages (e.g. Cewa)', explained as vowel lengthening; no Lunda-specific exception.
new_statements.domain_note: The statement is a generalization over 'Zambian languages' from a 25-variety survey that included Lunda (Ndembu) and Lunda (Ishindi); it is not a Lunda-specific paragraph. Word level implied ('syllables.. in the same word'); citation forms not discussed. Lunda-specific primary descriptions (Kawasha 2003; Fisher & Fisher 1963/1984) were not accessible and could supersede this.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement is a pan-Zambian generalization by Kashoki & Mann (1978) whose survey explicitly included Lunda (Ndembu) and Lunda (Ishindi) = lund1266 (recordings made in Solwezi and Mwinilunga, NW Province). Carvalho 1890 (also examined, penultimate 'accento tónico', p. 11) describes the Lunda of the Mwant Yav court = Ruund, ruun1238, and must not be credited to lund1266; likewise the Nash/Vincke/Hoover 'Lunda' resources named in ERIC ED256170 are Ruund.

sources.note: Sec. 3.4 'Tone and Stress', pp. 70-71: in Zambian languages (Lunda (Ndembu) and Lunda (Ishindi) are among the 25 varieties the authors studied, Table 2:1 pp. 28-29) syllables are 'more or less evenly stressed'; in some (e.g. Cewa) the penult seems slightly stronger but that is the lengthened syllable; stress never distinguishes words; every syllable carries tone (two contrastive tones, H and L; a Lunda tone-pair example 'bark of a tree' is given on p. 71). Pan-Zambian generalization, not a Lunda-specific paragraph.

sources.citation: Carvalho, Henrique Augusto Dias de. 1890. Methodo pratico para fallar a lingua da Lunda, contendo narrações historicas dos diversos povos. Lisboa: Imprensa Nacional.
sources.note: p. 11: 'O accento tónico recae quasi sempre na penúltima syllaba e por isso mesmo, com poucas excepções, os vocábulos são graves' (a few oxytones, e.g. dizêu 'tooth'; very few proparoxytones, e.g. tátuko 'father'). NOT lund1266: this is the Lunda of the Mwant Yav court = Ruund [rnd], ruun1238 (Glottolog tagging per the ruun1238 check record).

sources.note: Lunda appears only on pp. 202-203: no final /e, o/; pre-antepenultimate vowel shortening (ku-kwáat-a > ku-kwát-ish-il-a, elicited with Boniface Kawasha), i.e. contrastive length limited to penult and antepenult. No statement on Lunda stress.

sources.note: Syntax paper (pp. 38-42 read via Persée page text). p. 42: 'Subject relativisation is tonally marked. In Lunda, the high tone is assigned on the first syllable of the verb, while the first syllable of the verb in an independent clause carries a low tone.' Confirms Lunda is tonal; nothing on stress.

sources.quote: The first person singular and class 1 subject prefixes delete with this aspectual morpheme. The two are distinguished by tone. ... independent pronouns can stand alone as words, but possessive pronominal stems can only occur attached to agreement prefixes. In addition, the former bears a low tone and the latter carries a high tone on the first syllable.
sources.note: Syntax paper; states in passing that segmentally identical forms are distinguished by tone (na- with deleted 1sg vs class-1 subject prefix, p. 6 fn. 3) and that independent pronouns bear L while possessive stems carry H on the first syllable (p. 13). No tone inventory or rules; nothing on stress.
